results.title: IETF Protocol RFC Semantics
results.prompt: According to RFC 9110, what is the exact semantic difference between HTTP 401 Unauthorized and HTTP 403 Forbidden?
results.reply:
According to RFC 9110, the distinction comes down to authentication versus authorization.

A 401 Unauthorized response means the request lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource. Essentially, the server is saying it doesn't know who you are or your proof of identity was rejected. Because of this, a 401 response must include a WWW-Authenticate header to tell the client how to provide those credentials.

A 403 Forbidden response means the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it. This is used when the identity is known—or even if the request is anonymous—but the requester simply doesn't have permission to access that specific resource. Unlike a 401, repeating the same request with the same credentials won't change the outcome.

401 vs 403: Which HTTP Status to Return (and the Mistake Almost Everyone Makes)

401 vs 403: Which HTTP Status to Return (and the Mistake Almost Everyone Makes) WHATSAPP  ✅ EMAIL  ✅ Home About Architecture Notes Technical Articles Contact English Português Español Home 401 vs 403: Which HTTP Status to Return (and the Mistake Almost Everyone Makes) 401 is for not authenticated, 403 for no permission, and most people swap the two. A clear guide with a decision tree, the header RFC 9110 requires on a 401, and when 404 is the security choice. And how it shows up in OpenShift: 401 for the token, 403 for RBAC in oc. Posted by : Andre Rocha Date : 31 Aug, 2026 Category : REST API , Security 📖 Estimated reading time: 8 min ▶️ ⏹️ The rule fits on one line: 401 is not authenticated, 403 is authenticated but has no permission. Keep that and you are already ahead of more than half the APIs out there, because most swap the two. The trouble is the name gets in the way. 401 is called “Unauthorized”, which sounds like “no authorization”, but the RFC defines it around authentication . So “Unauthorized” really means “I don’t know who you are”. Add a detail that almost every API violates (the header 401 requires) and you have the recipe for confusion. Let’s untangle it, with RFC 9110 open beside us. The name is a trap Memorize the mnemonic and the rest follows from it: 401 = “who are you? prove it.” The server doesn’t know, or couldn’t verify, who is asking. Send a credential (or a better one). 403 = “I know who you are, and no.” The identity was accepted, the access was denied. Repeating with the same credential changes nothing. The name “Unauthorized” on 401 is a historical artifact, inherited from the earliest HTTP specs and never renamed. RFC 9110 keeps the name, but the semantics are authentication, with no middle ground. 401 in practice: and the header nobody sends Per section 15.5.2 of RFC 9110 , a 401 “indicates that the request has not been applied because it lacks valid authentication credentials for the target resource”. That covers three cases you hit every day, and all three are 401 , not 403 : No credential was sent. The credential came malformed or wrong. The credential expired or was revoked. An expired token is not a valid credential, so it’s 401 , and 403 stays out of it. And here is the part almost every API breaks. The same paragraph says, with a normative MUST: a server that generates a 401 MUST send a `WWW-Authenticate` header with at least one challenge . A 401 without WWW-Authenticate is non-conformant, full stop. Your JSON API with a bearer token owes the header too. You satisfy the MUST with one line: HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Bearer Content-Type: application/problem+json If the request did come with a credential and it was rejected as invalid (malformed, wrong, or expired), it’s still 401 : the RFC says the client MAY repeat with a fresh Authorization . In other words, 401 is the invitation to re-authenticate. 403 in practice: where the posts get it wrong Section 15.5.4 is short: a 403 “indicates that the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it”. Most articles stop here and sum it up as “authenticated but no permission”. That’s almost right, and the “almost” is where the mistake lives. The RFC is finer, on three points a senior needs to get right: 403 doesn’t require an authenticated client. The text says “if credentials were provided”, a conditional. An anonymous request can land a 403 too. What’s forbidden is repeating with the SAME credential. The RFC says the client SHOULD NOT automatically repeat with the same credential, but MAY try a different one. So “re-authenticating never helps” is too strong. The correct version is “repeating with the same credential won’t help”. The reason may have nothing to do with the credential. The resource can be forbidden by a business rule, an IP, a time window, whatever. And unlike 401 , a 403 does not require WWW-Authenticate , and in practice most ship without it. RFC 9110 does leave the door open to send the header on a 403 (section 11.6.1, a MAY) when a different credential would change the result, which lines up with point 2 above. Actually mandatory only on the 401 . Anyone who uses OpenShift hits this pair every week, and oc is honest about the distinction. Expired or invalid token? The credential was rejected, and you get 401 Unauthorized . Authenticated but without the right role? You get 403 Forbidden , with the classic message pods is forbidden: User ... cannot list resource "pods" . One says “I don’t know who you are”, the other says “I know who you are and you can’t”. OpenShift RBAC is one of the most didactic 403 machines around: if the 403 still feels abstract, run an oc get without permission and it shows up with a full name. Which one to return? Answer’s right here Rule of thumb: 401 if the server doesn’t know who you are, 403 if it knows and denies you anyway. Want to feel it before the table? Check the conditions in the widget and it hands you back the code, the required header, and the RFC section. Which HTTP status to return? Answer the conditions. The verdict shows the code, the required header, and the RFC section. The decision tree, with the RFC section Situation Code RFC 9110 Section Required header Malformed request, bad framing or misleading routing (not the trash can for auth errors) 400 Bad Request 15.5.1 none Well-formed, but no credential, or an invalid/expired one 401 Unauthorized 15.5.2 WWW-Authenticate (MUST) Identity accepted but no permission, or refused for another reason (applies to anonymous too) 403 Forbidden 15.5.4 none The resource’s existence is sensitive and you don’t want to leak it (403 -> 404 substitution, a MAY in 15.5.4) 404 Not Found 15.5.5 none Resource exists and responds, but doesn’t support this method 405 Method Not Allowed 15.5.6 Allow (MUST) A proxy in the path (not the origin) requires authentication 407 Proxy Authentication Required 15.5.8 Proxy-Authenticate (MUST) Server doesn’t recognize the method for any resource 501 Not Implemented 15.6.2 none When 404 is the security choice When the resource’s very existence is sensitive information. A 403 confirms the resource exists, it just denies access, and that leaks. A private repo, an object ID from another tenant, anything whose existence is itself sensitive: if you answer 403 , you’re saying “it exists, but it’s not yours”. Sometimes that’s exactly what the attacker wanted to know. The RFC saw this coming. Section 15.5.4 itself says an origin that wants to “hide” the existence of a forbidden resource MAY answer 404 instead. It’s a normative permission, not a suggestion. The 404 hides; the 403 confirms. Where existence matters, return a 404 that looks the same whether the resource doesn’t exist or exists but is forbidden. A caching detail: 404 is heuristically cacheable and doesn’t distinguish temporary from permanent. If you know it’s gone for good, 410 Gone says so better. The neighbors people mix up 400 is not a trash can. It’s for syntax, framing and routing (section 15.5.1). A well-formed but unauthenticated request is 401 ; authenticated with no permission is 403 . Throwing 400 at an auth failure is the classic one. 405 for the wrong method, with the Allow header. If the resource exists but doesn’t accept POST , it’s 405 (section 15.5.6), and the RFC requires the Allow header listing the methods that do work. Not 403 . 407 belongs to the proxy, never to your origin. Equivalent to 401 , but the one asking is a proxy in the path, with Proxy-Authenticate (section 15.5.8). An origin serving its own access control doesn’t emit 407 . 405 vs 501 : a known method not supported on this resource = 405 ; a method the server doesn’t recognize for any resource = 501 . The anti-pattern that breaks caches and clients: 200 with an error body Returning 200 OK with an {"error": ...} in the body looks harmless and is a trap. This isn’t a loose opinion, it’s citable mechanics: Caches, proxies and generic client libraries dispatch on the status class (the first digit), not on your JSON. RFC 9110 (section 15) says a client MUST understand the class of any status from the first digit. A 200 asserts success at the protocol level and is heuristically cacheable (sections 15.1 and 15.3.1). Under RFC 9111, a cache can store and re-serve that “success” with heuristic expiration, even with no freshness header. Translation: your error wrapped in a 200 can be silently cached and handed to other clients as if it had worked. RFC 9457 (Problem Details), section 3.1.2, shuts the door: generators MUST use the same status code in the actual HTTP response, precisely so generic software keeps working. Calling it an anti-pattern is my engineering conclusion, not a literal line from the RFC. But the mechanics it rests on are all citable. The correct pattern: a real 4xx / 5xx status, with the readable detail in the body, preferably application/problem+json . Run it yourself (reproducible PoC) A status code clicks once you see the response on screen. The lab below spins up a server (plain Node, no dependencies) that returns each code with the header the RFC requires, so you can check it with curl -i . git clone https://github.com/linuxelitebr/linuxelite-labs cd linuxelite-labs/http-status node server.js Watch the WWW-Authenticate on the 401 and the Allow on the 405 : curl -sD - -o /dev/null http://localhost:8080/needs-auth HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Bearer Content-Type: application/problem+json demo.sh hits every scenario (401, 403, 404-hidden, 405, 407-simulated) and shows the status and headers of each. Instructions in the lab README . The gotchas, straight up 401 = not authenticated (send WWW-Authenticate ). An expired token is 401 , not 403 . 403 = understood and refused. Doesn’t require an authenticated client, and applies to anonymous. On 403 , repeating with the same credential won’t help; with a different one, MAY. 404 hides existence; 403 confirms it. Where existence is sensitive, 404 . 400 is for syntax, not for an auth failure. 405 (with Allow ) for the wrong method, not 403 . 407 belongs to the proxy, not your origin. Never 200 with an error body. A generic cache doesn’t read your JSON. What comes next A status code is one piece of API design. Before you return the right error, you need to cache the right response, and that’s where another classic mix-up starts: no-cache doesn’t turn caching off , and s-maxage is not the CDN’s max-age . Which status burned you in production? I’d bet there’s a 401 -without- WWW-Authenticate story that left a client stuck in a loop.
